posts.title: Tuesday 3/17 - Mellow score on the way to Dunedin, south of a lighthouse. Long exploratory afternoon in Dunedin
posts.body:
As the sun came up, what resembled the rolling green hills of Upstate NY (the area around Christchurch) transformed into temperate tropical Mediterranean coastal bucolic magic. The van charged on through dawn, through vast expanses of sheep meadows and weird cypress trees. We pulled up on a gorgeous, glass, back-lit waist high beach break with nobody in sight—and decided to break the number one rule (“don’t leave fish to find fish”) by leaving this 7am beach break splendor to check out a lighthouse that may have had a point break.

The detour was an excellent sight-seeing decision but a poor surf guiding one. The lighthouse was painted white and barely cleared the variety of palms and other strange fake-looking real trees. Appeared to be, like many lighthouses, not technologically relevant due to its small stature and positioning set far back on the hill. Makes it a much more interesting lighthouse. Fur seals lined the bay and barked and laughed in the sun. Elsie enjoyed their company but I felt they were rubbing it in. We stopped for a quick photo shoot at the top of the hill and the headed back to the beach break.


We paddled out and had ourselves a mellow score of a session, which was the debut of Elsie’s custom and my handshape. Everybody happy. Board will take some getting used to, but has the potential for greatness. Squirts with speed in small stuff and flat sections but TBD in bigger stuff. Sampled a few fins and will likely end up where I started (K2 or some small keel). Elsie’s board is light, maneuverable, and importantly has what seems to be the right curves and concanves in the right places. Cool airplane takeoff feeling from the nose concave.


After making breakfast and coffee in front of the spot, we drove south, arriving in Dunedin in the afternoon. We landed at a break in town that was howling offshore. Checked a few spots on the peninsula that were way too windy but the act of checking was enjoyable — perched on a high headland, walked through a field of sheep.




Then checked Black Head, a spot south of Dunedin. Some barrel opportunities but few and far between and very windy. Did not paddle out.

St Paddy’s dinner in Dunedin at Italian spot in front of town surf spot St Clair. Chatted with bartender who was an American doing a postgrad in geology at U Otago. He had only been in NZ for a year, and had already adopted lots of the lingo. Also kind of sounded like he was forcing an accent which made us giggle.


Drove to Smaills beach lot to sleep — a spot on the peninsula — but was gusting so hard that the van tipping over was a genuine concern. We were so tired and delirious that when Elsie raised this issue, I said “yeah but at least we’ll tip sideways and not off the cliff”. We moved to a parking lot in front of St Clair, the break in town, shortly after. Full night’s sleep.

posts.title: Monday 3/16 - Arrived!
posts.body:
Long travel day included an 18 hour flight from JFK > AKL, one failed approach into Christchurch due to fog, doubled back to Auckland, and one successful landing. Met a surfer flying through to Brisbane who was an engineer on Qantas now spending his pension flight miles.

Picked up the van, loaded up on groceries, and picked up Elsie’s board, which she had custom made by a local dude. Drove through and out of Christchurch, which was aglow with a blanket of warm Indian Summer. Leaves had started to change but it was 70 and sunny. Slept at beach parking lot a few hours south of Christchurch.

posts.title: Blizzard Board & Whiplash Syndrome
posts.body:
Fueled by Ryan Burch podcasts and having scraped early 2000s era shaping forums, I left NYC at 10pm in a borrowed car (thank you Hutch) to pick up five surfboard blanks in New Jersey. The image of Steve Lis holding his rust-colored fish recurred in the center of my periphery like a double exposure photo overlaid on the road ahead.

My plan was to drive the blanks from Jersey through NYC to a basement shaping bay in Long Island (thank you Jack and Wolves) and show up at a glass shop in Brooklyn with a finished piece of foam on Sunday afternoon. I was fixated on this plan, overcome by it, and had actually rationalized that since it had become my mission to surf a hand-shape in New Zealand, I could bail on important social commitments I had made weeks prior.

Once the gratification of my name Sharpied onto five blanks wore off, and 11:30pm-in-Manasquan-fatigue set in, I started to consider whether my plan was compatible with a Friday event in SoHo. I had been here before. I knew that my attendance would mean a lot to someone. However, attending would mean one fewer day to figure out how to use a planer, shape rails that aren’t upside down, and make a board that’s more than two inches thick (all failures of my previous four attempts to shape surfboards). It would entail more prolonged anxiety of the variety I was already experiencing: I had the inescapable desire to surf a functional hand-shape halfway across the world, and it was entirely achievable.

I thought about the movie Whiplash. Early on, student drummer Andrew Neiman pre-empts an ugly breakup—of a relationship that hasn’t even begun—by conveying that his desire to be an excellent musician is incompatible with a life of pizza dates and movie nights. It’s actually quite rational. If you want to be the best, you have to drum until your hands bleed. And then keep drumming. There simply is no time or energy for anything else.

Surfers ask for a lot in their life. They ask for much more than entire days spent shirking responsibilities at the beach. There is one statement surfers are very comfortable with telling their friends and loved ones: “I’m not sure if I can, there might be waves.” Surfers are worse than Andrew Neiman because they want it both ways: to indulge their cravings to surf whenever they want, and have friends and loved ones that don't care about their noncommitment.

At the end of Whiplash, after months of trauma and accepting burnout, Neiman eventually learns that balance will bring him fulfillment. He accepts that he won’t become the next jazz great, and that’s okay because there are other things in life.

I re-routed my 2:30am arrival in East Hampton to a 12:30am arrival in NYC. I stuck around for the birthday party in SoHo. Elsie and I wore 2000s-themed clothes. I wore two t-shirts, a Marker fleece and hat, baggy jeans, and a shark tooth necklace. Elsie wore a dress over jeans and plastic jewelry from 15 years ago. It was sick. I had an amazing time, and I knew it was the right decision when I hit the road Saturday at 7am, en route to the shaping bay.

On Saturday, it took me 8 hours to complete a board. By my standards, every feature was perfect, except it was two inches thick. So, on Sunday, racing an historic blizzard headed forecast to hit New York, I duplicated the board, leaving a little more foam throughout. I measured very little and relied more heavily on instinct. It felt like a real surfboard on all sides.

The ride back was treacherous. I left Long Island around 4pm and within an hour, Hutch’s Cherokee was trudging through six inches of slush. Flakes fell violently, their paths warped by the car’s windshield like Star Wars and accumulated at two inches per hour. Several other drivers ended up inadvertently off-roading. I leaned on my phone contacts to keep me out of nonverbal road-staring trance. I arrived in Brooklyn four hours later with my piece of foam, a massive smile on my face, and lots of adrenaline from driving at 110% focus for four hours.

I picked up the finished product three weeks later, on a sunny March day 4 days ahead of departure for NZ. Aaron at (Kings Glassing) is a pro. His feedback on my shaping was overall positive, but I couldn’t help but fixate on “tail is a little thick and it might be hard to turn”. It put me back where I was a few weeks prior, feeling anxious about getting everything right. But then I thought of the relief, joy, presence I felt after deciding to stay in the city for one more night.

My goal was to surf a functional hand-shape in New Zealand. I’ll still surf a hand-shape in New Zealand, but maybe the tail will be a little thick.
